title: Cardiologist's Three Longevity Habits: Lp(a) Test, Strength Training, Treated Sleep Apnea
excerpt: Interventional cardiologist Dr. Sanjay Bhojraj says three underused steps — a one-time Lp(a) blood test, training for functional strength, and treating sleep apnea — can meaningfully slow how fast your heart ages.
body:
• Interventional cardiologist Dr. Sanjay Bhojraj's advice for aging more slowly: get lipoprotein(a) checked once, train for the physical abilities you'll want at 75, and get sleep apnea treated.
  • The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety dyslipidemia guideline gives a Class I recommendation that every adult have Lp(a) measured at least once in a lifetime.
  • Lp(a) is largely genetic and stable across life; elevated levels raise cardiovascular risk even when a standard cholesterol panel looks normal, with risk approximately doubling above 250 nmol/L.
  • Obstructive sleep apnea affects 40 to 80 percent of people with cardiovascular disease yet remains underrecognized; the American Heart Association urges screening in patients with resistant hypertension and related conditions.

The inherited risk hiding in a normal cholesterol panel

Dr. Sanjay Bhojraj, an interventional cardiologist and certified practitioner of the Institute for Functional Medicine, laid out his advice in an Instagram post on September 8: three things most people still are not doing that matter more than an occasional hard workout. Hindustan Times, reporting on the post, flagged that the content is user-generated and has not been independently verified — so it is worth checking each claim against published medical guidance. The first claim, it turns out, now sits at the center of a major guideline shift.

Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a type of LDL cholesterol that is largely genetic and stays relatively stable across a person's life. That stability is exactly the point: a single measurement tells you most of what you need to know. Elevated Lp(a) can raise cardiovascular risk even when the standard cholesterol panel looks reassuring, which is why it is sometimes called a hidden risk factor.

That framing is no longer a fringe view. The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on the management of dyslipidemia — the first U.S. cholesterol guideline to do so — recommends universal once-in-a-lifetime Lp(a) measurement in adults as a Class I recommendation, the strongest level a guideline issues. The guideline identifies elevated risk beginning at 125 nmol/L (approximately 50 mg/dL), with observational data suggesting cardiovascular risk may approximately double at levels above 250 nmol/L. As Dr. Roger Blumenthal, chair of the guideline writing committee and director of the Johns Hopkins Ciccarone Center for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease, explained when the guideline was released: a value in the 400 range is associated with about a quadrupling of long-term risk. Notably, Lp(a) testing is not part of a standard lipid panel and must be ordered separately.

"The advantage we have now is that we can see a lot of this risk earlier. I want my patients using this information at 45 or 55, while there's still plenty of time to do something useful with it."

— Dr. Sanjay Bhojraj, Interventional Cardiologist

Train for the things you'll want to do at 75

Dr. Sanjay's second recommendation shifts from the lab to the gym, and it reframes the goal of exercise: train for the physical capacities you will still want at 75. He cited a 2026 study of more than 13,000 adults over 65, which found that balance and agility, lower-body strength, and cardiorespiratory fitness were all strongly associated with lower mortality. "I care a lot less about whether someone can crush a workout once in a while and a lot more about whether their body is staying useful," he said.

That functional-fitness framing lines up with what global guidelines already advise. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening activities involving the major muscle groups on two or more days a week. For adults over 65, WHO adds balance-focused activity three or more days a week to prevent falls. The point is not novelty; it is that most people skip exactly these pieces.

Sleep apnea, the underdiagnosed heart risk

The third habit is the least obvious: get sleep apnea checked if you snore, wake up exhausted, or have blood pressure that refuses to behave. "Sleep apnea is widely underdiagnosed, and it shows up all over cardiology," Dr. Sanjay said. "Repeated oxygen drops and fragmented sleep night after night can affect blood pressure and metabolic health over time."

The American Heart Association's scientific statement in Circulation backs up the urgency. Obstructive sleep apnea occurs in 40 to 80 percent of people with cardiovascular disease, yet it is often underrecognized and undertreated in cardiovascular practice. The AHA recommends screening for OSA in patients with resistant or poorly controlled hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, and recurrent atrial fibrillation after cardioversion or ablation. "Obstructive sleep apnea can negatively impact patients' health and increase the risk of cardiovascular events and death," said Dr. Yerem Yeghiazarians of UCSF, chair of the statement's writing group.

Why this matters especially for South Asians

For the Indian diaspora, the Lp(a) point deserves particular attention. Population studies have repeatedly found elevated Lp(a) more common among South Asians than in many other populations — one reason preventive cardiologists urge diaspora families not to be reassured by a "normal" cholesterol report alone. A single Lp(a) test in midlife, paired with honest management of the modifiable risks (blood pressure, blood sugar, activity, weight), is the combination the new guidelines push toward. And snoring that the whole household jokes about is worth a conversation with a doctor rather than a shrug, particularly when hypertension runs in the family.

What to do with this information

None of these steps requires a radical life overhaul. Ask your primary-care doctor whether an Lp(a) test should be added at your next blood draw — many commercial insurance plans cover it, though coverage as a preventive service varies and some patients face cost-sharing. Add two days of resistance work to whatever aerobic routine you already have. And if you snore loudly, wake unrefreshed, or cannot get blood pressure under control, ask about a sleep assessment rather than accepting exhaustion as normal aging.
